title: How logins work
summary: What really happens when someone logs in: password hashing, "Sign in with Google" and magic links, and the mistakes that leak accounts.
youWillLearn: Why an app should never store a password, and what it stores instead
What salt and a slow hash add, and why bcrypt or Argon2 beat a plain hash
How Sign in with Google works without Notely ever seeing the Google password
How magic links work, and what to check on the login form itself

glossary.authentication: Proving who you are, for example by typing the right password. Deciding what you may do comes later.
glossary.hash: A fixed-length fingerprint computed from some input. The same input always gives the same hash, and you cannot turn the hash back into the input.
glossary.salt: A random value stored next to each user's hash and mixed into it, so two people with the same password get different hashes.
glossary.bcrypt: A password hashing function that is slow on purpose, with an adjustable cost. Argon2 and scrypt are newer siblings built for the same job.
glossary.OAuth: A standard that lets one app act on, or log you in with, your account at another service, without ever getting that service's password.
glossary.OpenID Connect: The login layer on top of OAuth. It adds a signed statement of who the user is, which is what "Sign in with Google" uses.
glossary.identity provider: The service that checks the password and vouches for the user: Google, Apple, GitHub, or your own auth server.
glossary.redirect URL: The address an identity provider sends the user back to after login. It must be on a list you registered in advance.
glossary.magic link: A login link sent by email. It holds a long random token that works once and expires after a short time.
glossary.credential stuffing: Bots trying email and password pairs leaked from other sites, hoping people reused them on yours.
glossary.MFA: Multi-factor authentication: a second proof after the password, like a code from an authenticator app.

steps.title: Never keep the password itself
body: Maya signs up for Notely with her email and a password. A quick first draft saves the password as-is in a users table. Logins work fine.
Then the database leaks: a stolen backup, a bad query, a hacked laptop. The attacker now holds every password in plain text. People reuse passwords, so Maya's Gmail is at risk too.

callout.text: A leak is not a rare disaster you can plan around. Assume your database will be copied one day, and make sure the copy is useless.

scene.caption: The password goes straight into the table. One leaked backup exposes everyone.

steps.title: Store a fingerprint, not the password
body: Notely never needs to read Maya's password again. It only needs to check that she typed the same one.
So at sign-up it stores a hash: a one-way fingerprint of the password. At login it hashes what she typed and compares. Same fingerprint: she is in. That check is authentication.

callout.text: A fingerprint can prove a person was here, but you cannot rebuild the person from it. A password hash works the same way.

scene.caption: The table now holds fingerprints. Login hashes the typed password and compares.

steps.title: Salt and slowness: the real recipe
body: A plain hash is not enough. Two users with password123 get the same hash, and attackers keep huge lists of common passwords already hashed.
So each user gets a random salt mixed in. And the hash function is slow on purpose: bcrypt, scrypt or Argon2. One login barely notices. A billion guesses become very expensive.

code.caption: $2a$ means bcrypt, 10 is the cost. Salt and hash live in one string. Same password, different strings.

callout.text: Never write your own hashing. Let the auth provider do it, or use a well-known library for bcrypt or Argon2.

scene.caption: Same password, different salts, different hashes. A precomputed list no longer helps.

steps.title: Sign in with Google: no password at all
body: Better still: do not hold passwords. With Sign in with Google, Google checks the password and tells Notely who logged in. Google is the identity provider.
The standard behind this is OAuth, and its login layer is OpenID Connect. Notely never sees Maya's Google password, so it cannot leak it.

callout.text: A hotel that accepts your passport instead of issuing its own ID card. It trusts the government already checked who you are.

scene.caption: Maya logs in at Google. Notely's database holds no password for her.

steps.title: The redirect dance, step by step
body: 1. Notely sends Maya's browser to Google. 2. She logs in and approves. 3. Google sends her back to Notely's redirect URL with a one-time code. 4. Notely's server trades that code with Google for her verified identity.
The code works once, expires fast, and is useless without a second proof Notely kept back.

scene.caption: Google returns a one-time code. Notely's server trades it for Maya's identity.

steps.title: Redirect URLs must be on a list
body: Google, and Supabase in front of it, only send codes back to redirect URLs you registered in advance. That stops an attacker from having Maya's code delivered to their own site.
The classic bug: login works on localhost, then fails in production or on Vercel preview URLs, because nobody added those addresses to the list.

callout.text: Do not "fix" a failing redirect with a wildcard that matches any domain. Add the exact production URL, and keep any preview wildcard tied to your own team's domain.

scene.caption: Google only hands codes to addresses on the list. Anything else is refused.

steps.title: Magic links: the inbox is the key
body: Another password-free option: Maya types her email, and Notely sends a magic link. It holds a long random token that works once and expires soon. Clicking it logs her in.
The trade-off: whoever can read Maya's inbox can log in as her. That was already true, since every "forgot password" email works the same way.

scene.caption: Notely emails a single-use link. Clicking it brings the token back to the server.

steps.title: Notely hands all of this to Supabase
body: Notely writes none of this logic itself. Supabase Auth hashes passwords with bcrypt, runs the Google flow and sends magic links. Notely calls one function per method.
After any of them succeeds, Supabase gives the browser proof that Maya is logged in. How that proof works is the next lesson, Sessions vs tokens.

callout.text: Ask: does any of our own tables have a password column? (It should not.) Does anything log request bodies on login routes? Are the production and preview URLs in Supabase's Redirect URLs and Google's console? Does /auth/callback call exchangeCodeForSession?

scene.caption: Three login methods, one auth service. Notely's own tables hold no passwords.

steps.title: The login form leaks too
body: Error messages: "No account for this email" tells an attacker who uses Notely. Say "Wrong email or password" for both cases.
Unlimited tries: bots run credential stuffing, replaying leaked email and password pairs from other sites. Rate-limit login attempts, and offer MFA so a correct password alone is not enough.

callout.text: You met rate limiting in system design. A login form is one of the first places it belongs, counted per account and per IP address.

scene.caption: A bot hammers the login form with leaked passwords. Rate limits and MFA stop it.

steps.title: Recap in one breath
body: Never store passwords. Store a salted, slow hash (bcrypt, scrypt, Argon2), and compare hashes at login. Better: let an identity provider like Google check the password, through OAuth and OpenID Connect, or email a single-use magic link.
Either way, use a proven auth service, register exact redirect URLs, and rate-limit the login form.

quiz.question: Claude Code drafts a profiles table with a password column and plans to compare it with what the user types. What do you ask for instead?

options.text: Encrypt the column with a key stored in an env var.
options.why: Encryption can be reversed by anyone who gets the key, and the server needs that key at hand. Passwords should never be recoverable at all.

options.text: Hash it with SHA-256 before saving.
options.why: Better than plain text, but SHA-256 is fast and unsalted here. Attackers can test billions of guesses per second against it.

options.text: Drop the column and use Supabase Auth, which stores salted bcrypt hashes.
options.why: A proven auth service salts and slow-hashes passwords for you, and keeps them out of your own tables.

quiz.question: "Sign in with Google" works on localhost but fails on the production site with a redirect error. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: The production URL is missing from the allowed redirect URLs.
options.why: Google and Supabase only send users back to addresses registered in advance. Add the exact production URL to both lists.

options.text: Google blocks logins from sites hosted on Vercel.
options.why: Google does not care where a site is hosted. It only checks that the redirect URL is on your registered list.

options.text: Maya's Google password is not stored in production yet.
options.why: Notely never stores Google passwords. Google checks the password itself.

quiz.question: A client wants to drop passwords and use only magic links. What changes about the account's security?

options.text: Nothing can go wrong, because there is no password to steal.
options.why: The link itself is now the key. Anyone who reads the inbox, or intercepts the link before it expires, can log in.

options.text: Account safety now depends on the user's email inbox.
options.why: Whoever controls the inbox can log in. This was already true for password resets, so it is often a fair trade.
You can and should limit how often links are requested per email and per IP, so the form cannot be used to spam inboxes.

takeaways: Never store passwords. Store a salted, slow hash (bcrypt, scrypt or Argon2) and compare hashes at login.
Do not write your own auth. Let Supabase Auth or another proven service hash, verify and email for you.
Sign in with Google uses OAuth and OpenID Connect: Google checks the password, your app gets a verified identity.
Register exact redirect URLs for production and previews. Avoid wide wildcards.
Use one vague error for wrong email or password, rate-limit logins, and offer MFA.
